Hook: In the early 1970s the San Francisco Bay Area was building a railway, BART, and planners had to say how many people would ride it. The official forecast, from a model of the trips between zones of the map, said about fifteen percent of work trips. Daniel McFadden tried something else. Before a single train ran, he took a survey of commuters: how long each trip took by car and by bus, what it cost, and what each person chose. From those choices he estimated how much a minute and a dollar mattered to them, and used that to forecast a choice they had never had. His model said 6.3 percent. When BART was running, in 1975, it carried 6.2 percent. McFadden went back to the same travellers to check.

That is what this part is about. Start with choices people actually made. Write a model in which those choices come from hidden quantities: what a minute, a dollar, the future or a risk is worth to them. Find the values of those quantities that make the model's predictions match the choices, and say how sure you are. Then ask the model about a world nobody has seen: a new railway, a new tax, a new pension. It works only if the hidden quantities stay put when the world changes, and only if the data really pin them down. Both of those can fail, and this part shows how to tell.

The question: how is a model's hidden machinery measured from the choices it predicts? What makes a model's parameters worth measuring at all? How are they measured: by likelihood, by moments, by simulation? What in the data pins down which parameter? And how would we know if the answer were wrong?
Economics, Built. Part fifty-four: estimating models.

By the end of this part you will be able to say what makes a model structural, and why a forecast of a new policy needs one; how maximum likelihood, the generalized method of moments and simulation estimate its parameters, with standard errors; which facts in the data pin down which parameters, and how to check; where calibration, sufficient statistics, validation against experiments and bounds fit in; and you will have watched all of it done on the Island, where the truth is known, so every estimate can be graded.
Structural: Economists use the word structural a great deal. Jacob Marschak gave it its meaning in 1953: to predict the effect of a policy that has never been tried, you must measure the things the policy will not change. A reduced-form forecast takes a history, finds a pattern in it, and extends the pattern. That is fine while the world stays as it was. A structural forecast goes from choices to what produced them, preferences and constraints, and then asks how the same people, with the same preferences, would choose under the new policy. Robert Lucas's critique, from Part twenty-eight, is the warning: a pattern fitted under one policy can break under another, because the pattern was itself a response to the old policy.

Here is the difference on the Island, where we know the truth. For twelve years the price of fuel moved the cost of a car trip up and down by a dollar or so, and each year a share of the Island's three thousand commuters drove. A straight line fits that history well: each extra dollar, about ten points fewer drivers. Now the town proposes a congestion charge of 8 dollars a trip, far outside anything in the history. The line says minus 33 percent of commuters would drive: fewer than none. The logit we will estimate in the next chapter models each commuter's choice, so the share can never fall below zero; as the charge rises, fewer and fewer drivers are left to lose. It says 2.1 percent. The truth is 2.7 percent. The line was not wrong about the past. It was never a model of why people drive, so it had nothing to say about a world it had not seen.
Logit: Chapter two. Random utility and maximum likelihood.

McFadden's model starts from a person, not a zone. Commuter i gets some utility from each way of getting to work. Part of it we can see: the minutes and the dollars, weighted by how much each matters, and a constant for what the option is like. Part of it we cannot: the weather that morning, a dislike of buses, a bag to carry. Each commuter takes whichever option gives more. If the unseen parts are independent draws from the extreme-value distribution, the chance of taking the bus has this simple form, a logistic curve in the difference between the two options' visible utilities. That is the logit. Now turn it round. For any guess at the weights, the model gives each commuter a probability of doing what they actually did. Multiply those together over everyone, or add the logarithms, and you have the likelihood. Maximum likelihood takes the weights that make the choices people actually made most probable.

The Island has 3,000 commuters, each with a car trip and a bus trip of different lengths and costs. Group them by how much better the bus looks, under the fitted model, and plot the share in each group who took it. The logit's curve runs through them. Where the bus looks much worse, almost nobody takes it, but not quite nobody: the unseen part of utility means some people always surprise us. That is what the model's randomness is for.

Here is the log likelihood as a landscape over the two weights, with the constant held at its estimate. Bright is high. The top is a narrow ridge: people's choices say clearly how minutes trade against dollars, and a little less clearly how much both matter. Newton's method climbs it from zero by fitting a bowl to the surface where it stands and jumping to the bowl's top. It arrives in 5 steps. The white cross is the truth we planted; the gold dot is the estimate. And the curvature at the top gives the uncertainty: a sharp peak means the data pin the parameters down, a flat one means they do not. Its inverse is the estimate's variance, Fisher's information at work.

The estimates. Each lies within one and a half standard errors of the value we planted. The number transport planners most want is a ratio: how many dollars a commuter will pay to save an hour, sixty times the weight on a minute over the weight on a dollar. The estimate is 6 dollars 96 an hour, give or take 0.41, against 7 dollars 20 planted. That is a price nobody ever posted, read off the choices people made. It is the number that goes into every appraisal of a new road or railway.

Now the reason for all this: a forecast. The Island opens a railway, 35 minutes and 2 dollars 50 for everyone. Before it, the commuters split between car and bus. The logit, given the railway's time and fare and its constant, forecasts that rail takes 44 percent of commuters. In fact it takes 43 percent, close. But look where its riders come from. The logit says 58 percent of them leave the bus and the rest leave their cars; in truth 67 percent leave the bus, and 30 percent still drive, not 25 percent. The logit's hidden assumption is that a new option draws from the old ones in proportion to their shares, because the unseen parts of utility are independent. On the Island, people who dislike the car's alternatives dislike both of them: rail and bus are close substitutes. McFadden's nested logit of 1978 lets the unseen parts be correlated within a nest. A forecast of traffic on the roads depends on getting that right.
GMM: Chapter four. The generalized method of moments.

Maximum likelihood needs the whole probability model. Often an economic model tells you less, but something sharp: some quantity should be zero on average. Write those as moment conditions: functions of the data and the parameters whose expectation is zero at the true parameters. Lars Peter Hansen's generalized method of moments, of 1982, takes the sample averages of the conditions and chooses the parameters that make them as close to zero as possible, measured with a weighting matrix W. With more conditions than parameters, they cannot all be zero exactly, and the weighting matters. The best weights are the inverse of the conditions' covariance: noisy conditions count less, and conditions that move together are not counted twice. The variance of the estimate follows from how fast the conditions respond to the parameters. And because the extra conditions are over-identifying, the minimized objective is itself a test, Hansen's J: if the model is right, it is roughly chi-squared, with as many degrees of freedom as extra conditions.

The most famous use is Hansen and Kenneth Singleton's, from the same year. A household that can save in an asset gives up a unit of consumption today only if it expects the return, valued in tomorrow's marginal utility and discounted, to repay exactly one unit. That is Part twenty-three's Euler equation. Multiply it by anything the household knew at the time, and the average must still be zero: each instrument gives a moment condition. On the Island we have 2,000 periods of consumption growth and returns on two assets, a bond-like one and a risky one; with a constant and last period's values as instruments, that is eight conditions for two parameters. Here is the GMM objective over patience and risk aversion, bright where it is small. The estimates: beta 0.969, risk aversion 2.90, against 0.97 and 3 planted. Notice what we did not do: we never solved for the household's consumption rule, or said what its income process was. The Euler equation alone was enough. Notice, too, the long bright ridge: more patience and more risk aversion can stand in for each other, and the two estimates are strongly correlated. We met that ridge in the Play it, and we will meet it again.

Now the test. With two assets there are six more conditions than parameters, so if the model is right, J should look like a draw from the green curve. It is 11.3, below the five percent line: the model is not rejected. Now add a third asset whose return is 1 percentage point a period higher than the model can explain: a premium the household's Euler equation does not price. There are now thirteen extra conditions, and J jumps to 67, far beyond the red line. The model is rejected. Two cautions. A rejection says the conditions cannot all hold at once; it does not say which one fails. And when Hansen and Singleton took the model to American stock returns, several of their specifications were rejected, an early sign of the trouble Part twenty-three called the equity premium puzzle.
Simulate: Chapter five. When the likelihood has no formula.

The logit had a formula for each choice's probability. Most realistic models do not. Let tastes vary from person to person, or let today's choice depend on expectations about tomorrow, and the probability of what someone did becomes an integral nobody can write down. But you can still simulate the model. In 1989 Daniel McFadden, and separately Ariel Pakes and David Pollard, showed how to estimate with simulations. Guess the parameters. Simulate the model several times, S data sets as large as the real one. Compute their moments, compare them with the data's, and adjust the guess until they match: the method of simulated moments. Two rules. Use the same random draws at every guess, or the objective jumps about and no optimizer can climb it. And pay for the simulation in precision: with S simulated data sets, the variance of the estimate is multiplied by one plus one over S. This is the workhorse behind random-coefficient demand in Part forty-three, dynamic choice in Part forty-four, and the life cycle in the next chapter.

Indirect inference, from Christian Gouriéroux, Alain Monfort and Éric Renault, and from Anthony Smith, goes one step further. Take a moving average: each period's value is a fresh shock plus theta times the last one. It is trivial to simulate, but its likelihood is awkward to write. So look at the data through a lens that is easy to fit: a regression of each value on its three predecessors, by least squares. The lens is the wrong model, and that does not matter. Choose theta so that the same lens, fitted to data simulated from the model, sees the same coefficients. In this sample of 200 periods, indirect inference gives 0.59; the simplest method, inverting the first autocorrelation, gives 0.66. The truth is 0.5.

One sample proves nothing, so repeat it 300 times. Here is the spread of the simple estimate across samples: centred on the truth, but wide, with a typical error of 0.13. And indirect inference: centred on the truth too, and about half as wide, a typical error of 0.07. The first autocorrelation uses one feature of the data; the lens uses three, and the simulations translate them back into the parameter. Choosing a good lens is choosing which features of the data the estimate listens to, the same question the Play it asked.
LifeCycle: Chapter six. The Island's households, estimated.

Now a full example, done the way Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas and Jonathan Parker did it for American households in 2002, but on the Island, where we planted the answer. The household is Part twenty-two's: it works from twenty to fifty-nine on a risky income, then lives on a pension to sixty-nine. Each year it chooses how much to consume, saves the rest at three percent, and cannot borrow. Two numbers are hidden: patience and caution. The data are 3,000 households' average consumption at ten ages and their wealth at six: sixteen moments. For each guess at the two numbers, the computer solves the household's problem backwards from the last year, simulates 5 populations with fixed draws, and compares their moments with the data's.

Here is what is being matched. On the left, consumption by age: it rises through the working years as incomes grow and the households build a buffer, peaks in the late thirties, and falls as the impatient households spend down. On the right, wealth: almost nothing at forty, a hump that peaks just before retirement, then run down through the pension years. The purple lines are the model at the estimated values. They pass through every point: sixteen facts matched with two numbers.

The search started far away, at patience 0.93 and caution 3. After 138 guesses, each one a solved and simulated economy, it stopped at patience 0.9505 and caution 1.95, against 0.95 and 2 planted: each within about one and a quarter standard errors of the truth. The J statistic, 6.4 on 14 degrees of freedom, says the model fits, as it should: it is the model that made the data. And here is the warning from the Play it, in one number. The two estimates' correlation is minus 0.9999. The sixteen facts pin down a line of patience-and-caution pairs very precisely; what picks a point on the line is the subtle curvature of the profiles. With real data, where the model is never exactly right, that is a thin thread to hang a number on.
Types: Chapter seven. Dynamic choices and hidden types.

When today's choice changes tomorrow's options, the model has to look ahead, and so does the estimator. For each guess at the parameters, solve the dynamic problem for the value of each choice in each state, turn the values into choice probabilities, and evaluate the likelihood of what people did. That is John Rust's nested fixed point, which estimated the bus engines of Part forty-four. Joseph Hotz and Robert Miller found a shortcut: read the values off the observed frequency of each choice, and skip most of the solving. And Michael Keane and Kenneth Wolpin estimated young men's careers this way, with one more ingredient that turns out to matter enormously: a few hidden types of person.

Here is why. The Island follows 800 commuters for 8 weeks. Each week each of them takes the bus or not, depending on how the trip looks that week. The bars count people by how many weeks they took the bus. We planted two kinds of people: 40 percent who dislike the bus, in pink, and the rest, who like it, in green. The data do not say who is which. And we planted no habit at all: last week's choice has no effect on this week's.

Now estimate. Ignore the types, and fit one logit to everybody. The response to how the trip looks comes out at 0.63, too small: the hidden differences between people add noise that flattens it. Worse, add last week's choice as a regressor, and it comes out at 1.16, more than twenty standard errors from zero: a strong habit that does not exist. People who took the bus last week are mostly the people who like the bus. James Heckman called this spurious state dependence. Now let there be two hidden types, and estimate their share and their constants along with everything else. The EM algorithm asks, person by person, how likely each type is given everything they did, refits, and repeats. It finds the response, 0.85, the share of bus-haters, 0.40, and a habit of 0.10: about zero. The difference matters. If riding builds a habit, a free week of buses is a good investment; if it does not, it is a gift to people who would have ridden anyway.
Identify: Behind every estimate is a question that has nothing to do with sample size. A parameter is identified if, with unlimited data, only one value of it would fit. Tjalling Koopmans and the Cowles Commission put the question at the centre of econometrics from 1949. The Play it showed a weak case: four facts that leave a whole line of values almost equally good. Rust's buses showed another: the discount factor barely moves the likelihood. What identifies a parameter is variation in the data that moves its footprint and not the others'. And in practice the useful question is: which moments is this estimate leaning on? Isaiah Andrews, Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro answered it with one matrix, built from the same pieces as the standard errors. It says how far each estimate moves when each moment moves a little.

Here it is for caution, in the Island's life-cycle estimate. Each bar is one of the sixteen facts: consumption at ten ages in blue, wealth at six in pink. Its height is how far the estimate of caution would move if that one fact in the data were one percent higher. The standard error of the estimate is 0.04. The bars are enormous by comparison, and they alternate in sign. One percent more wealth at sixty-five moves it by minus 5.7; one percent more wealth at sixty, by 3.5. The efficient estimate is reading tiny differences between facts that move almost together, the line from the Play it, and amplifying them.

So test it. Suppose the survey overstated every household's wealth by one percent, a tiny error by the standards of any real survey. Adding up the pink bars, the matrix predicts that caution's estimate moves by minus 1.45. Estimating the whole model again, it moves by minus 1.50: the matrix was right, and it took no new estimation to know. That shift is 38 standard errors. A standard error measures how much the estimate would vary with a new sample from the same world. It says nothing about an assumption that is slightly wrong. The sensitivity matrix shows which assumptions matter, and a careful paper reports it beside the estimates.
Calibrate: When Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott built the first real business cycle model in 1982, they did not estimate it. They calibrated it: each parameter was taken from other evidence, a long-run average or a study of households, and the model was then judged on things it had not been built to match, like how much consumption moves over the cycle. Lars Peter Hansen and James Heckman replied, in the same journal issue of 1996, that borrowed numbers come from other models and other populations, and that a model whose parameters are never confronted with the data cannot be told it is wrong. The modern practice is a compromise: calibrate what is well measured elsewhere and estimate the rest, or let the outside evidence enter as a prior, as the Bayesian estimation of central banks' models does. On the Island we can see what the choice costs.

Suppose we calibrate caution, taking it from the Dial of relative risk aversion, and estimate only patience. The left panel is the best patience for each calibrated caution. They trade off along the ridge: calibrate caution at one, as studies of consumption and labour supply suggest, and patience comes out at 0.961; calibrate it at four, from surveys of gambles over lifetime income, and patience is 0.927. The borrowed number decides the estimated one. But the data are not silent. The right panel is how badly each pair fits, on a log scale. Only near caution two does the fit pass the test: at one the J statistic is 529, at four 2417, against 8 at two. So calibration hides nothing if you also report the fit; it misleads when the borrowed number is simply assumed, and the profiles the model was meant to explain are never looked at again.
Sufficient: Structural estimation asks a lot: every primitive of the model, measured. Raj Chetty pointed to a shortcut. For many policy questions, the welfare effect of a small change depends only on a few numbers that can be measured directly. Part forty-two's formula for unemployment insurance is the example: a slightly higher benefit is worth it if the gain, the drop in consumption when people lose their jobs valued in marginal utility, exceeds the cost, the elasticity of unemployment to the benefit. The formula holds in any model that produces those two numbers, whatever the details of search, saving or borrowing. Chetty called these sufficient statistics: a bridge between structural logic and reduced-form evidence.

Check it on Part forty-two's model, where we know everything. On top, welfare computed from the whole model, for every benefit level. Below, the formula, computed at each benefit from just the two numbers an economist could measure there. They agree: the formula crosses zero exactly where welfare peaks, at 33 percent of the wage. Nothing else about the model was needed.

What it cannot do. Suppose the one experiment we have was run at a benefit of 20 percent of the wage, and measured an elasticity of 0.18. To find the best benefit, the formula needs the elasticity at other benefits too. Assume it is the same everywhere, and the formula puts the best benefit at 50 percent, against 33 in truth. In the model, the elasticity rises steeply as benefits rise: the closer the benefit comes to the wage, the larger the share of what a job adds that each further rise takes away. Sufficient statistics answer local questions without a model; for a change far from the data, you need to know how the statistics themselves would move, and that is a model again.
Validate: Chapter eleven. Validation: predict the experiment.

How would we know if a structural model were wrong? The strongest test is to predict an experiment before looking at it. In 1997 Mexico began PROGRESA, which paid mothers when their children attended school, and started it first in villages chosen at random. Petra Todd and Kenneth Wolpin estimated a model of families' schooling choices using only the control villages, where there was no subsidy. How can data without a subsidy say what a subsidy does? Through wages. Children's wages differ from village to village, and a school subsidy works like a cut in the wage a child gives up by attending. If families treat a peso of subsidy like a peso of wages, the model can predict the subsidy's effect. They predicted the treated villages' schooling, then compared. The predictions were broadly close to what the experiment found. And once validated, the model could answer what the experiment could not, like how a different schedule of payments by age would have done.

The Island runs the same test. 200 villages of 60 children; half, chosen at random, get a subsidy for attendance. A schooling model estimated on the control villages alone, where children's wages vary, predicts that the subsidy raises attendance by 18.2 points. The experiment finds 18.1. Validated. Now a second world, identical except that parents respond to the subsidy more than to the same money in wages, because it is labelled for school, or because it comes with a condition attached. The model, estimated as before, still predicts 18.2 points. The experiment finds 30.3. The prediction fails, and its failure is informative: the assumption that a peso is a peso, which let wages stand in for a subsidy, is what broke. A model that passes such a test has earned some trust; one that has never faced one has not.
Bounds: Chapter twelve. Bounds instead of points.

Every method so far ended with a point and a standard error. Charles Manski asked what we know before we assume anything. Every point estimate rests on assumptions the data cannot check. So start with none, see what the data alone say, and add assumptions one at a time. The answer is an interval, the set of values consistent with the data and the assumptions made so far, and it narrows as the assumptions grow stronger. Manski called the trade-off the law of decreasing credibility: the stronger the assumptions, the sharper the answer and the less anyone should believe it.

Back to the Island's school experiment, with a complication: attendance records are missing for about 20 percent of children, and nobody knows why. With no assumption at all, a missing child might or might not attend, so the subsidized villages' attendance lies between 53 percent and 72 percent, and the control villages' between 37 percent and 59 percent. So the effect lies between minus 6 percent and 35 percent: the data alone cannot even say the subsidy helped. Add one assumption most people would accept: the children with missing records attend no more often than those with records, since registers tend to lose the dropouts. Now the effect lies between 5 percent and 28 percent: positive. The usual analysis assumes the records are missing at random and reports a single number, 18 percent. It happens to be close to the truth here, but its attendance rates are not: they are several points too high, because the missing are mostly the dropouts. The white ticks are the truth, inside every interval that only assumed what was true.
Frontier: Simulated moments search for the parameters anew for every data set. The frontier turns that around. Draw a parameter at random, simulate a data set from the model, summarize it, and do this thousands of times. Then learn the map from summaries back to the parameter that produced them: with a regression here, with a neural network at scale. For the moving average, after 3,000 simulated samples, the learned map estimates 300 fresh ones with a typical error of 0.06, and each estimate takes no search at all. Kyle Cranmer, Johann Brehmer and Gilles Louppe call the family simulation-based inference; it learns whole posterior distributions, not just points, and economists have begun to use it for structural models whose simulations are too slow to search through.

What remains open. Learned estimators are fast but approximate, and their errors have to be checked against known truths, which is what a simulated world like the Island is for. Machine learning is moving inside estimation: flexible models for the parts of a problem we do not care about, with the structural parameter kept in view. Models and experiments are being combined: estimate on one arm and predict the other, as Todd and Wolpin did, or let an experiment pin down the parameter the observational data cannot. And John Horton and others have asked language models to answer surveys and play economic games, as simulated people. Whether their answers say anything about real people's parameters is, so far, a question for validation, not an answer.
